boy1: Why does neck pain happen, how long does it last, and does a straightened neck matter? Six exercises to do at home, desk tips, videos and warning signs.
boy2: Almost everyone has it at some point in their life. It is usually not caused by anything serious, but it often comes back. The good news: with regular movement and the right exercises, it can largely be kept under control.

boy7: Pain returns within 1–5 years after a first episode
boy8: Neck pain is pain anywhere from the base of the skull down to the shoulders. It usually comes from the muscles, the ligaments and the small joints between the vertebrae. Doctors call this mechanical or non-specific neck pain: the pain is real, but there is no serious disease behind it.
boy9: If the pain spreads into your arm and fingers with numbness, tingling or electric-shock sensations, a nerve root may be involved. We cover this on a separate page: Cervical disc herniation and pinched nerve →
boy10: Staying in the same position for hours: working at a desk, bending over your phone for long periods
boy11: Your neck being strained for a long time while you sleep, or a "crick" that comes on with a sudden movement
boy12: Stress, anxiety and poor sleep: they increase muscle tension and sensitivity to pain
boy13: Lack of activity and weak shoulder and upper back muscles
boy14: Age-related wear in the spine (osteoarthritis). Many people with no pain at all have this finding too.
boy15: Sudden whiplash-type injuries, such as in a traffic accident
boy17: Physiotherapy guidelines divide neck pain into four groups. Treatment is shaped accordingly.
boy19: The familiar "crick in the neck". Your neck will not turn in some directions, and the pain gets worse when you move. This is the most common type.
boy21: Pain spreads from the neck to the back of the head, sometimes to the forehead, and is set off by neck movements. This is called cervicogenic headache.
boy22: With pain spreading into the arm
boy23: A nerve root is affected. There is pain, numbness, tingling or weakness in the arm.
boy26: Mostly seen after a traffic accident. The neck muscles lose some of their coordination and endurance.
boy27: About a straightened neck and "bad posture"
boy28: Seeing "straightening of the neck" on an X-ray report worries many people. A study compared 107 people, 54 with neck pain and 53 without, and found no difference in neck curvature between the two groups. According to the researchers, findings like this are not the cause of the pain but incidental changes.
boy29: Posture is a similar story: there is no single "correct posture" for everyone. The best posture is the one you change often. The problem is usually not the position itself, but staying in the same position for too long.
boy30: Most neck pain does not need an X-ray or MRI; the diagnosis is made through an examination. Treatment is planned according to the type of pain and how long it has lasted.
boy31: Bed rest and wearing a neck collar for long periods are not recommended. Carrying on with your daily activities as far as the pain allows speeds up recovery.
boy32: This is the cornerstone of treatment. Exercises that strengthen the neck, the shoulders and the muscles around the shoulder blades have been shown to reduce long-lasting neck pain moderately to markedly. Stretching exercises on their own may not be enough.
boy33: Mobilisation and manipulation of the neck and upper back, combined with exercise, improve pain and movement. They should be done by a trained physiotherapist after an examination.
boy35: Guidelines list these among the supportive options for long-lasting neck pain. They are worthwhile alongside exercise, not on their own.
boy36: Painkillers recommended by your doctor can give short-term relief.
boy38: When pain lasts a long time, managing stress and getting regular sleep are also part of treatment. Take a look at breathing exercises →
boy39: Six basic exercises for your neck
boy40: Do the exercises slowly and with control. A mild stretch is normal, but do not push into sharp pain. If the pain starts to spread into your arm, stop that exercise and talk to your physiotherapist.
boy42: Keep your shoulders still. Slowly turn your head to the right and hold for 2–3 seconds at the furthest comfortable point, then turn to the left in the same way.
boy44: Place your palm on your forehead. Without moving your head, push gently into your hand while your hand pushes back. Repeat for the back and both sides of your head. Half your strength is enough.
boy46: Looking after your neck at your desk
boy47: Hours spent in front of a screen are one of the most common triggers of neck pain. Small changes make a big difference.
boy48: Have the top edge of the screen at eye level or slightly below.
boy49: If you work on a laptop for long periods, use a laptop stand and a separate keyboard.
boy50: Raise your phone to eye level; lower your eyes, not your head.
boy51: Every half hour, get up, roll your shoulders and walk a few steps.
boy52: When you are on the phone, do not wedge it between your shoulder and your ear.

boy58: How long does neck pain last?
boy59: Most neck pain eases noticeably within days or a few weeks. However, it tends to come back: more than half of people who have it once get it again within 1–5 years. That is why it is important to keep up the exercises even after the pain has gone.
boy60: Should I use heat or cold?
boy61: For a stiff neck and muscle tension, gentle warmth helps most people. If you have had a recent knock or there is swelling, cold may be better in the first few days. Use whichever brings relief, for no more than 15–20 minutes, and protect your skin with a cloth.
boy63: There is no single best pillow for everyone. Choose a height that keeps your head level with your shoulder when you lie on your side, and does not push your head forwards when you lie on your back. Sleeping on your front can make the pain worse, because it keeps your neck turned to one side for a long time.
boy64: Should I wear a neck collar?
boy65: Not for ordinary neck pain. Wearing one for a long time can weaken the muscles and slow down recovery. After an accident, or when your doctor specifically recommends one, it is a different matter.
boy66: Do I need an X-ray or an MRI?
boy67: For most neck pain, no. Age-related wear and tear is common in people with no pain too, and often does not explain the pain. If you have one of the warning signs below, or the pain has not improved within a few weeks, your doctor will decide.
boy69: On its own, usually not. A reduced neck curve is common in people without pain too, and no link with pain has been shown. What matters are your symptoms and the examination findings.
boy70: Neck pain is usually harmless. However, see a doctor without delay if:
boy71: The pain started after a traffic accident, a fall or a blow
boy72: You have loss of strength in your arms or legs, clumsy hands (difficulty doing up buttons) or unsteadiness when walking
boy73: There has been a change in your bladder or bowel control
boy74: The pain comes with fever, chills, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer
boy75: You have severe night pain that keeps getting worse and does not ease with rest
boy76: You have a sudden, very severe headache, neck stiffness and a fever (call 112)
boy77: You also have dizziness, double vision, or difficulty speaking or swallowing (call 112)
boy78: Your neck pain comes with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating (it may be your heart; call 112)
